acceptedDateForms.note: Every one of these is the 8th of September 2026, written the way some teacher somewhere actually writes it. A form that is refused sends a teacher back to retype a hundred dates, so the list is generous on purpose.

cases.why: The tab they were looking at comes across, so they get the column they had on screen rather than whichever tab happens to be first.

A 'published to the web' link looks right and serves HTML forever. Told apart by the identifier being exactly 'e', and answered with its own message rather than 'that is not a Google Sheet link', which a teacher looking at a Google Sheet link will not believe.

googleSheetLinks.note: A teacher pastes the address from their browser. The address that hands back CSV is a different one, derived so nobody has to know that. The published-sheet link is the single most likely thing to go wrong and has its own answer.

note: How a teacher's own list of class dates is read — typed, pasted, from a CSV, from a calendar export, or from a Google Sheet. All of it is pure input to output, so all of it is portable. See contracts/README.md; the reasoning behind the rules is in documentation/.

cases.why: Not understood, and refused rather than guessed: a date guessed wrong dates a class wrong, silently.

TODAY COUNTS. The contract's today is a Tuesday, and a teacher asking on Tuesday for Tuesday's class means the class they are about to teach, not the one a week away - the same reading a person gives it. This is the case that fails if a platform decides a named day must always be at least a day off, which is defensible in the abstract and wrong every Monday morning.
Tomorrow, reached by its name instead.

Forwards, within the next seven days: the Monday coming, six days off, never the Monday just gone. 'Publish Monday's class' is said while preparing; a teacher who means a class already taught has its Unit and Day in front of them and says so.
The far end of the week still lands inside it.
Casing is the teacher's, not the matcher's. Compared as a day of the week rather than as a formatted name, so a machine whose language is not English still reads it.
The apostrophe belongs to the phrasing, not to the day. Both spellings of it, because which one a teacher types depends on their keyboard and on what autocorrect did to it.

Refused for the same reason as 'next Thursday' above, and named here because it is the near miss of a day that IS understood: 'next Monday' can mean the coming Monday or the one after it, people genuinely disagree about which, and the model answers it with today's date in front of it.
A day, not a habit. Nothing in the product means one class by it, so it is refused rather than read as the nearest thing that parses.

relativeDays.note: The words that reach the tools literally, because the card phrasings that carry them are matched in code and never sent to the model. 'Tomorrow' arriving as the word 'tomorrow' has to be understood where it lands. The seven weekday names arrive the same way, from the eight fixed 'publish <day>'s class' phrasings, and mean the NEXT such day counting today. WHERE the word is understood is a platform matter and deliberately not pinned here: both apps now settle the word where the call is made AND understand it in the tool, by different routes. The mac settles it in AssistAgent as the call is created - which covers a date the model filled in as well as a card's word - and its runner still reads one, for MCP callers with no card. Windows settles it in AssistCardCommand.ToJsonObject at match time, because its binder would drop an argument the tool does not declare, and understands it in the tool as well for the same reason. Neither may CAPTURE the day: a runner or a server that outlives a calendar day must read the clock per call, or a window left open across midnight publishes yesterday's answer and reports success. What both must agree on is which day the word names, which is what these cases are.

cases.name: a day past 12 settles the column as day-first
cases.why: 24 cannot be a month, so every row reads day-first — including 08/09, which alone is ambiguous.

cases.name: a month past 12 settles it the other way
wholly ambiguous columns ask
cases.why: Every row reads both ways. The question quotes the teacher's OWN value back and offers both readings in words — 'the 8th of September' against 'the 9th of August' — because a dialog asking about 'date ordering' is asking about a concept nobody has.

slashOrdering.note: 08/09/2026 is ambiguous on its own and both readings are somebody's convention. The rule: the COLUMN settles it, not the row. One value with a day past 12 anywhere in the column decides every row in it, and the teacher is not asked. Only a column where every row could be read either way becomes a question — and it is a question, not a refusal, because nothing is wrong with the teacher's file.

tabIdentifier.note: The gid a Sheets address carries, from either the query or the part after the #.
